laintiff Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission” or the “SEC”) files 
this Complaint against Defendants Xue Samuel Lee a/k/a “Sam” Lee (“Lee”) and Brenda Indah 
Chunga a/k/a “Bitcoin Beautee” (“Chunga”), and alleges as follows: 
SUMMARY 
1. This case involves a global, crypto asset-related, multi-level marketing pyramid
and Ponzi scheme that raised over $1.7 billion from victims worldwide, including millions from 
U.S. investors.  Defendants and others operated the scheme through a series of projects referred 
to collectively herein as “HyperFund.”         
1 The address for Defendant Lee reflects his last known address in Australia.  As indicated infra, we believe 
Defendant Lee currently resides in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. 
2 The address for Defendant Chunga reflects her known address during the actions set forth in the 
Complaint.  Ms. Chunga can be reached through her counsel:  Jonathan P. Van Hoven, 36 South Charles Street, 
Suite 901, Baltimore, MD  21201. 
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 1 of 31
2 
 
2. The HyperTech Group, a purported blockchain technology conglomerate  
founded by Lee and others (collectively, the “Founders”) launched HyperFund in June 2020.  At 
the outset, HyperFund claimed to be a project dedicated to creating a so-called “decentralized 
finance (DeFi) ecosystem” for crypto asset market participants.  Over time, the project’s stated 
goals evolved and utilized various names in an effort to capitalize on the buzz words and 
zeitgeist of the day, including rebranding itself as “HyperVerse” and, later, as “HyperNation,” a 
version of the project which featured an individual in a mask discussing creating a decentralized 
government to escape the societal bonds of inequality and injustice through blockchain 
technology.  HyperFund, including its subsequent rebranded iterations, is now defunct.   
3. From June 2020 through May 2022, HyperFund offered so-called “membership” 
packages promising exorbitant passive returns, supposedly derived in part from HyperFund’s 
crypto asset mining operations.  For example, HyperFund promised returns of 0.5% to 1% per 
day, with the prospect of tripling ones’ initial investment in 600 days.  HyperFund also 
implemented a pyramid scheme-like referral system to reward existing members for recruiting 
new investors.   
4. HyperFund’s membership packages were offered and sold as investment  
contracts, and therefore, securities under the federal securities laws, because investors made an 
investment of money in a common enterprise with a reasonable expectation of profits from the 
efforts of Defendants or third parties.  The membership packages were offered and sold without 
registration, and without qualifying for any exemption from registration. 
5. Lee was centrally involved with HyperFund throughout its lifecycle.  Lee was a 
co-founder of HyperTech Group, which claimed to be involved in “Large Scale Crypto Mining,” 
including bitcoin, that promoters asserted was a key revenue source for HyperFund.  However, 
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 2 of 31
3 
 
Lee later admitted that HyperTech Group was not engaged in large-scale bitcoin mining.  Lee 
was also featured prominently during HyperVerse’s launch event, and he even claimed to be 
helping to resurrect HyperVerse after its collapse, as a way of recouping investor losses.   
6. Chunga (known online by her nickname “Bitcoin Beautee”) was one of 
HyperFund’s top promoters and arguably the face of its United States presence.  Chunga’s 
recruitment efforts through online seminars and videos included the typical promotional ruses 
associated with fraudulent multi-level marketing schemes.  Here, that included focusing on 
investors’ supposed ability to make money via daily passive rewards, and also via so-called 
“accelerated” rewards if investors convinced others to join.  Chunga’s pitch was successful.  
Within six months, Chunga earned the highest level a HyperFund promoter could achieve, 
which, according to promotional materials, required at least $5 million in new investments, 
which were referred to as “sales,” and she continued to generate additional new investments long 
after that.  Chunga received over $3.7 million, both from the platform and directly from 
investors.  She used her earnings to fund extravagant personal expenses and help recruit others 
into the scheme by showing off the potential wealth to be earned through HyperFund.   
7. HyperFund, however, was a pyramid and Ponzi scheme.  HyperFund had no  
real source of revenue other than funds received from investors, and Defendants had no basis for 
the promised returns.  HyperFund did not engage in large-scale crypto asset mining, despite the 
claims by promoters like Chunga that the investors’ passive rewards were being paid by such 
efforts.  HyperFund even hired an actor to pretend to be the new CEO when HyperVerse was 
launched.  With no apparent legitimate source of revenues, investor withdrawals were paid with 
new investor deposits.    
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 3 of 31
4 
 
8. Chunga ignored red flags about HyperFund and made several misrepresentations  
to investors to convince them to join.  Lee knew or recklessly disregarded that the presentations 
used by the promoters, like Chunga, included false statements.  Lee also made statements to 
investors that were misleading by omitting material information about the nature of the business.  
Ultimately, the scheme collapsed in 2022 when investors were no longer able to make 
withdrawals.   
9. From approximately June 2020 to approximately November 2022, Defendants (1) 
raised millions of dollars from retail investors in the United States, and several other countries, 
through the unregistered offer and sale of securities styled as membership interests in 
HyperFund; and (2) made materially false and misleading statements about the investments and 
knowingly or recklessly engaged in a scheme to defraud investors—bilking the investors out of 
over $1.7 billion—by enticing them with the false promise of guaranteed, high returns from 
investments in securities. 
JURISDICTION AND VENUE 
10. The Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to Sections 
20(b), 20(d), and 22(a) of the Securities Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 77t(b), 77t(d), and 77v(a); and

12. In addition, this Court has jurisdiction because some or all of the Defendants

13. In connection with the conduct alleged in this Complaint, Defendants, directly  
and indirectly, singly or in concert with others, have made use of the means or instrumentalities

Group launched HyperFund.  HyperTech Group was featured in presentations as the business 
experience and expertise behind the project to give HyperFund credibility for prospective

17. HyperFund is the name of the multi-level marketing project launched by

FACTS 
A. Chunga and Lee Offered and Sold Securities Through HyperFund 
The Global Launch of HyperFund 
18. On June 11, 2020, in a press release issued through a paid service, the  
HyperTech Group announced that it was launching HyperFund.  The press release billed 
HyperFund as an “upgrade of HyperCapital,” a similar multi-level marketing project one of 
HyperFund’s Founders attempted to launch six months earlier, in January 2020.   
19. The press release described Lee as the founder and Chairman of HyperFund and  
listed Lee as the “contact” for inquiries.  
20. In the press release, Lee was quoted as saying that the upgrade reflected a change  
in the strategic focus and development plans of the company.  The press release claimed 
HyperFund would be “more streamlined and better equipped to handle the challenges and 
opportunities in the traditional finance and cryptocurrency market” and would have three key 
focus areas: tech incubation, investment and funding, and community building. 
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 6 of 31
7 
 
21. The press release also claimed that HyperTech Group planned to be listed on the 
Hong Kong Stock Exchange by 2022 and that it intended to launch products such as HyperNews, 
HyperTalk, and HyperShow, supposedly blockchain-based social networking platforms.      
22. The presentations Chunga later used to recruit investors similarly prominently 
featured these and other details about the Founders, including Lee, and the entities that 
purportedly comprised the HyperFund Group on slides that were labeled “Credibility,” including 
slides featuring screenshots of Lee appearing on CNN and other media outlets.  One of the 
details Chunga touted was the fact that Lee and another one of the Founders were featured and 
interviewed in an episode of an Amazon Prime documentary series called “Next: Blockchain.”      
23. In one presentation, Chunga leveraged HyperFund’s Founders’ public-facing  
profiles in order to persuade investors that there was no risk in investing with the HyperTech 
Group:  
Some people say things, how do we know they won’t just take our money and 
disappear?  Well, ladies and gents, they have more to lose than to gain. They’re 
all over CNN.  They have publicly traded companies, they are on Amazon Prime, 
their faces are everywhere.  They have more to lose than to gain.   
 
24. As Chunga emphasized in other presentations: “[L]adies and gents, this is not a  
company that needs your money. . . .  He doesn’t need us.”  (emphasis added).   
25. On information and belief, Lee was not only a co-founder of HyperFund, but he  
maintained control over HyperFund throughout its existence.  Lee’s background and role as co-
founder of HyperFund was a prominent feature of the marketing and promotional materials used 
by promoters to attract new investors.  Lee was aware or recklessly disregarded that 
HyperFunds’s marketing materials used to recruit investors contained material misstatements 
because he admitted as much during a call with an investor.  Lee also recorded a message that 
was released as part of the launch of HyperVerse in December 2021, and later appeared in video-
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 7 of 31
8 
 
teleconference calls with promoters and others to attempt to assuage the concerns of 
HyperFund’s investors.  
HyperFund’s “Membership Rewards” Program 
26. Investors purchased “memberships” in HyperFund at various levels using the 
crypto asset Tether (USDT).  For example, in her HyperFund videos, Chunga encouraged 
investors to “Choose Your Membership” level:  $300, $500, $1,000, or $10,000.  Typically 
HyperFund promoters, including Chunga, gave a link to investors through which the investors 
would use Tether to purchase the package.  On the HyperFund platform, the value of the 
individual’s membership level was reflected in the form of an internal value called HyperUnits, 
or HU.  For example, a $300 membership was reflected as 300 HyperUnits.   
27. Chunga told investors who purchased a membership that they would receive:  (1)  
access to a crypto asset educational platform; (2) exclusive pre-sale offerings of future crypto 
asset projects, such as, initial coin offerings (“ICOs”) at 20%-30% below market value; and (3) 
automatic returns on their investment, which were called “rewards.”  
28. HyperFund offered two ways for members to make money:  passive rewards, 
which promised investors a daily return of 0.5% to 1% of the value of their investment until they 
earned triple the value of their initial investment, and leveraged or accelerated rewards.     
29. As Chunga explained in a promotional video recorded on or about February 9, 
2021, “[Y]ou will receive your initial membership in 6.5 months, lets round it up to 7 months. . .   
You now have your initial investment amount back in your pocket.  And then what happens after 
that?  Everything else that’s coming to you every day after that, what is that?  That is pure profit.  
You did not have to work for it.”  
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 8 of 31
9 
 
30. According to Chunga, “here, with HyperFund, your money is doing all of the 
work for you and you don’t even have to get out of bed.”   
31. Investors could supposedly also earn “accelerated” rewards by recruiting new 
investors which promoters, like Chunga, encouraged HyperFund investors to do.   
32. HyperFund offered three types of leveraged rewards:  Community Rewards, VIP  
Rewards, and Global Rewards.  First, with respect to Community Rewards, Chunga explained in 
her presentations that, in exchange for building the community by referring HyperFund to friends 
and family, HyperFund would supposedly pay investors 20% of their downline’s membership 
value every day up to 20 levels.  HyperFund’s “COMMUNITY REWARD” program was

membership in your entire team, they are going to now pay you an additional one

36. Chunga frequently encouraged investors to increase their membership value by 
reinvesting their rewards through so-called “rebuys” instead of withdrawing them, including in

37. HyperFund’s structure further discouraged withdrawals.  The only way to  
withdraw the rewards was to convert the internal HyperUnits to so-called “Molecular Future” 
(MOF)—a crypto asset issued, in part, by another founder of HyperFund (“Founder B”)—and 
then transfer the MOF from the HyperFund platform to the HOO Exchange, which was a digital

38. Although the so-called HyperUnits were reflected on the HyperFund platform as

arguments.text: SEC complaint alleges HyperFund was a global crypto-asset MLM pyramid and Ponzi scheme raising over $1.7bn; launched June 2020 by HyperTech Group, rebranded HyperVerse around Dec 2021 and HyperNation around May 2022, and defunct. Membership packages promised 0.5%-1% daily returns and tripling in 600 days, with referral rewards. Complaint alleges no legitimate revenue, no large-scale mining, withdrawals funded by new deposits, and investor collapse in 2022. It alleges HyperTech hired an actor to pretend to be HyperVerse CEO. Sam Lee was centrally involved/co-founder and later admitted HyperTech was not engaged in large-scale bitcoin mining. Brenda Chunga/Bitcoin Beautee was a top promoter, reached top level requiring at least $5m in new investments, received over $3.7m, and used wealth display to recruit. HyperUnits bought with Tether were converted to MOF via HOO Exchange, with withdrawal value not pegged and MOF quoted at $0.00001949 on 2023-09-04. Chunga's presentations emphasized founders' CNN/Amazon visibility as credibility and low risk. DOJ page says Lee was charged with conspiracy to commit securities and wire fraud; Chunga pleaded guilty to same; Rodney Burton/Bitcoin Rodney was charged with unlicensed money-transmitting offenses. DOJ says alleged $1.89bn scheme, aliases HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, HyperNation, claimed 0.5%-1% passive rewards from nonexistent mining, and withdrawals began to be blocked at least July 2021. CNBC reports same charges and Chunga settlement. Guardian reports Steven Reece Lewis was introduced as CEO at Dec 2021 launch with claimed Leeds/Cambridge degrees, Goldman Sachs work, sale of web company to Adobe, and IT startup; Guardian found no records at those organizations/registries and no internet presence beyond promotion. Celebrity Cameo-style support videos from Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass promoted HyperVerse; no suggestion celebrities knew model. Guardian describes $300 minimum, 0.5% daily and 300% over 600 days, multilevel commissions to 20 levels, migration to HyperNation after withdrawal problems, masked Mr H/Miss N ambassadors, and a promoter describing HyperVerse/HyperNation as one big entity. Lee denied involvement in HyperNation and disputed founder role; these are responses/allegations, not independently resolved.

# Final OSINT Report: HyperFund / HyperVerse Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence describes HyperFund—later associated with the names HyperVerse and HyperNation—as an alleged global crypto-asset pyramid and Ponzi scheme. According to the SEC complaint, the operation raised more than **$1.7 billion** through membership packages that promised unusually high daily returns and rewarded investors for recruiting additional participants. The DOJ characterized the criminal case as involving an alleged **$1.89 billion** cryptocurrency fraud scheme. These figures differ slightly by source and should not be treated as a single independently verified total. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

The alleged recruitment model combined:

1. **High-return investment promises**—including advertised daily returns of 0.5% to 1% and potential doubling or tripling of principal.
2. **Multi-level referral incentives**—including commissions linked to direct and multi-level recruitment.
3. **Credibility marketing**—emphasizing founders’ media appearances, public profiles, and purported business affiliations.
4. **Public promoters**—particularly Brenda Chunga (“Bitcoin Beautee”) and Rodney Burton (“Bitcoin Rodney”).
5. **Rebranding and migration**—from HyperFund to HyperVerse and later HyperNation.
6. **A questionable CEO persona**—Steven Reece Lewis, whose qualifications and employment history could not be verified by the Guardian, while the SEC complaint alleges an actor was hired to pose as HyperVerse’s CEO.
7. **Withdrawal restrictions and token conversion mechanisms**—which allegedly made it difficult for investors to recover the nominal value of their holdings.

The criminal charges and SEC allegations are not equivalent to final judicial findings against every defendant. The DOJ expressly notes the presumption of innocence. Brenda Chunga, however, pleaded guilty according to the DOJ and CNBC reports. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 1. Identity and organizational continuity

### HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation

The SEC complaint states that HyperFund was launched by the HyperTech Group in June 2020, rebranded as **HyperVerse** around December 2021, and later as **HyperNation** around May 2022. The DOJ describes the alleged network as also known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

This supports treating the names as successive or associated iterations of one alleged operation, rather than clearly separate enterprises. The SEC described the projects collectively as “HyperFund,” while the DOJ used a set of associated names. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

### Rebranding pattern

The SEC alleges that the project’s stated goals changed over time and used different contemporary themes, including decentralized finance, the metaverse, and a decentralized government concept associated with HyperNation. [SRC-004]

The Guardian reported that members experiencing withdrawal problems were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. A senior promoter reportedly described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” although that characterization came from the promoter and is not independently established by the source. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The available evidence supports a pattern of continuity through renaming and migration. It does not, by itself, establish the precise legal or corporate structure connecting each iteration.

---

## 2. Alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Promised returns

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund membership packages promised returns of **0.5% to 1% per day**, with the possibility of tripling the initial investment in 600 days. [SRC-004]

The Guardian similarly reported a minimum membership of **$300**, a minimum return of 0.5% per day, and a purported 300% return over 600 days. [SRC-003]

The DOJ states that promotional materials allegedly promised daily passive rewards of 0.5% to 1% until the investor’s initial investment was doubled or tripled. [SRC-002]

### Claimed source of returns

According to the SEC and DOJ allegations, promoters claimed that returns were supported in part by large-scale cryptocurrency mining operations. The SEC complaint alleges that:

- HyperTech was promoted as a crypto-mining and blockchain-technology group.
- Sam Lee later admitted that HyperTech was not engaged in large-scale bitcoin mining.
- HyperFund had no legitimate revenue source sufficient to support the promised returns.
- Investor withdrawals were allegedly funded with deposits from newer investors. [SRC-004]

The DOJ likewise states that the alleged mining operations did not exist. [SRC-002]

**Assessment:** If the allegations are proven, the claimed mining-based revenue model would have functioned as a credibility narrative rather than the actual source of investor payments. The alleged use of new investor deposits to satisfy withdrawals is the central Ponzi-like mechanism described by the SEC.

---

## 3. Recruitment and multi-level marketing structure

The evidence describes two overlapping ways investors were allegedly encouraged to participate:

- Passive rewards for purchasing a membership.
- Accelerated or leveraged rewards for recruiting additional investors.

The SEC complaint alleges that investors purchased memberships using Tether, receiving internal “HyperUnits.” It describes community, VIP, and global reward programs tied to recruitment and organizational volume. One alleged community program paid rewards based on a downline extending up to 20 levels. [SRC-004]

The Guardian likewise reported that members received HyperUnits for recruiting new members, with referral commissions calculated according to the number of recruits and additional recruits made by those participants, extending down to 20 levels. [SRC-003]

The SEC complaint also alleges that promoters encouraged “rebuys,” in which members reinvested rewards instead of withdrawing them. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The alleged structure combined investment returns with recruitment-based compensation. That combination is consistent with the pyramid-scheme characterization made by the SEC and DOJ, although the legal determination depends on the relevant court proceedings.

---

## 4. Token and withdrawal mechanics

The SEC complaint alleges that:

1. Investors used Tether to purchase membership packages.
2. Their account balances were represented internally as HyperUnits.
3. To withdraw, HyperUnits had to be converted into MOF.
4. MOF had to be transferred through the HOO Exchange and converted into other crypto assets before being exchanged for fiat currency.
5. HyperUnits were initially represented as pegged to a dollar value, but the MOF conversion was not pegged at that value.
6. MOF was quoted at approximately **$0.00001949** on September 4, 2023, according to the complaint. [SRC-004]

The DOJ alleges that investor withdrawals began to be blocked by at least July 2021. [SRC-002] CNBC also reports that the scheme collapsed in 2022. [SRC-001]

**Assessment:** The described architecture could create a substantial gap between an investor’s nominal account balance and the realizable withdrawal value. It also introduced additional conversion steps and platform dependencies, potentially increasing friction and limiting liquidity. The evidence establishes these allegations and reported mechanics, but does not independently establish the full transaction history of each investor.

---

## 5. Public promoters and credibility-based recruitment

### Brenda Chunga / “Bitcoin Beautee”

The SEC identifies Brenda Chunga, also known as **“Bitcoin Beautee,”** as one of HyperFund’s top promoters and a prominent figure in its U.S. promotional activity. The complaint alleges that:

- She promoted daily passive rewards and accelerated rewards.
- She reached the highest promoter level within six months.
- That level allegedly required at least $5 million in new investments referred as “sales.”
- She received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors.
- She used apparent wealth and extravagant personal spending to help recruit others. [SRC-004]

CNBC reports that Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud and separately agreed to settle SEC civil charges. [SRC-001] The DOJ also states that she pleaded guilty. [SRC-002]

The SEC complaint further alleges that Chunga’s presentations used founders’ public profiles and media appearances as credibility signals. The presentations reportedly emphasized CNN appearances, publicly traded companies, Amazon Prime exposure, and the argument that the founders had “more to lose than to gain.” [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** Chunga appears in the evidence as both a high-volume recruiter and a credibility amplifier. Her alleged use of visible wealth and founder publicity illustrates how the scheme could convert social proof into investment confidence.

### Rodney Burton / “Bitcoin Rodney”

The DOJ identifies Rodney Burton, also known as **“Bitcoin Rodney,”** as a promoter of HyperFund. He was charged with conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money-transmitting business and operating an unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

The available benchmark material provides less detail about Burton’s specific recruitment messaging than it does about Chunga. His alleged role should therefore be described as a promoter and charged participant, without attributing additional tactics not documented in the sources.

---

## 6. The questionable CEO persona

### Steven Reece Lewis

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis was introduced as HyperVerse’s CEO at a December 2021 online launch event. Promotional material attributed to him claimed:

- A University of Leeds degree.
- A master’s degree from the University of Cambridge.
- Employment at Goldman Sachs.
- The sale of a web-development company to Adobe.
- The creation of an IT start-up. [SRC-003]

The Guardian states that it found:

- No record of Steven Reece Lewis at the University of Leeds or University of Cambridge.
- No record under that name in UK Companies House or SEC records.
- No Adobe filing showing acquisition of a company owned by him.
- No Goldman Sachs employment record.
- No LinkedIn profile or meaningful internet presence outside HyperVerse promotional material. [SRC-003]

The Guardian also reported that the account in his name appeared shortly before the launch, promoted HyperVerse for approximately six months, and then became inactive. [SRC-003]

Separately, the SEC complaint alleges that HyperTech hired an actor to pretend to be the new HyperVerse CEO. The complaint does not, in the supplied text, independently prove that Steven Reece Lewis was the actor; that connection should therefore remain an allegation or unresolved inference. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The evidence supports describing the CEO identity and credentials as **questionable and unverified**, not as conclusively fabricated. The strongest formulation is that the Guardian could not verify the claimed background and the SEC separately alleged the use of an actor as a supposed CEO.

---

## 7. Celebrity and public-image promotion

The Guardian reported that HyperVerse released support videos featuring:

- Steve Wozniak
- Chuck Norris
- Jim Norton
- Lance Bass [SRC-003]

The reported messages encouraged support for HyperVerse and praised or endorsed Steven Reece Lewis’s leadership. The Guardian noted that all four individuals were available through Cameo, a service allowing users to commission personalized videos, and that the messages appeared during a broader recruitment push. [SRC-003]

The Guardian explicitly stated that there was **no suggestion these celebrities knew the underlying business model**. The videos did not refer to investments or money, according to the report. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The videos could function as social-proof and legitimacy signals even if the participants did not understand or endorse the alleged investment mechanics. The evidence supports the existence of the promotional videos, but not intentional participation in fraud by the celebrities.

---

## 8. Collapse and investor harm

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund collapsed in 2022 when investors could no longer make withdrawals. [SRC-004]

The DOJ alleges that withdrawal blocking began by at least July 2021. [SRC-002]

The Guardian reported that thousands of people lost millions of dollars and cited a Chainalysis estimate of approximately **$1.3 billion in consumer losses during 2022**, although that estimate is presented by the Guardian and is distinct from the SEC’s alleged amount raised. [SRC-003]

The SEC alleges that the operation raised more than $1.7 billion, while DOJ and CNBC describe the criminal case as involving approximately $1.89 billion. These figures may reflect different methodologies, periods, or legal allegations. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 9. Integrated assessment: how the alleged system worked

The benchmark evidence supports the following investigative model:

1. **Credibility construction:** HyperTech, its founders, claimed mining operations, media appearances, celebrity videos, and a purported CEO were used to present the project as technologically sophisticated and socially validated. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

2. **High-return proposition:** Investors were offered unusually high, largely passive daily returns and the prospect of doubling or tripling principal. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

3. **Recruitment expansion:** Investors were encouraged to bring in friends, family, and downline participants, with multi-level commissions and additional rewards. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

4. **Retention and reinvestment:** “Rebuys” and internal account balances encouraged investors to leave funds within the system rather than withdraw. [SRC-004]

5. **Liquidity restriction:** Withdrawal required conversion through internal units, MOF, and an associated exchange, while the alleged value of the internal units was not maintained during conversion. [SRC-004]

6. **Rebranding during distress:** As withdrawal problems emerged, the operation shifted from HyperFund to HyperVerse and then HyperNation, preserving an apparent sense of continuity or renewal. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

7. **Narrative replacement:** The project’s stated themes shifted from DeFi and mining to the metaverse and a masked, quasi-political “new world order” presentation. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Overall assessment:** The evidence depicts an alleged recruitment-driven financial system in which high promised returns, referral incentives, public-facing personalities, celebrity association, changing brand identities, and an apparently unverifiable executive persona collectively reduced investor skepticism and supported continued inflows. The SEC and DOJ allegations describe the economic core as dependent on investor deposits rather than legitimate mining revenue. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

---

## 10. Key uncertainties and limitations

- The SEC complaint contains allegations, not final findings on every factual issue. [SRC-004]
- The DOJ states that criminal defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. [SRC-002]
- The SEC’s alleged total of over $1.7 billion and the DOJ/CNBC figure of approximately $1.89 billion are not identical and should not be merged without qualification. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]
- The Guardian’s inability to verify Steven Reece Lewis’s credentials does not alone prove that the identity was fictitious.
- The SEC allegation that an actor was hired to pose as CEO does not, in the supplied evidence, conclusively identify Lewis as that actor. [SRC-004]
- The celebrity videos establish promotional association, not knowledge of or intent to support the alleged fraud. [SRC-003]
- The available evidence gives substantially more detail about Brenda Chunga’s promotional activity than Rodney Burton’s specific messaging.

7. **Withdrawal restrictions and token conversion mechanisms**—which allegedly made it difficult for investors to recover the nominal value of their holdings.

The criminal charges and SEC allegations are not equivalent to final judicial findings against every defendant. The DOJ expressly notes the presumption of innocence. Brenda Chunga, however, pleaded guilty according to the DOJ and CNBC reports. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

## 1. Identity and organizational continuity

### HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation

The SEC complaint states that HyperFund was launched by the HyperTech Group in June 2020, rebranded as **HyperVerse** around December 2021, and later as **HyperNation** around May 2022. The DOJ describes the alleged network as also known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

This supports treating the names as successive or associated iterations of one alleged operation, rather than clearly separate enterprises. The SEC described the projects collectively as “HyperFund,” while the DOJ used a set of associated names. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

### Rebranding pattern

The SEC alleges that the project’s stated goals changed over time and used different contemporary themes, including decentralized finance, the metaverse, and a decentralized government concept associated with HyperNation. [SRC-004]

The Guardian reported that members experiencing withdrawal problems were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. A senior promoter reportedly described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” although that characterization came from the promoter and is not independently established by the source. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The available evidence supports a pattern of continuity through renaming and migration. It does not, by itself, establish the precise legal or corporate structure connecting each iteration.

---

## 2. Alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Promised returns

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund membership packages promised returns of **0.5% to 1% per day**, with the possibility of tripling the initial investment in 600 days. [SRC-004]

The Guardian similarly reported a minimum membership of **$300**, a minimum return of 0.5% per day, and a purported 300% return over 600 days. [SRC-003]

The DOJ states that promotional materials allegedly promised daily passive rewards of 0.5% to 1% until the investor’s initial investment was doubled or tripled. [SRC-002]

### Claimed source of returns

According to the SEC and DOJ allegations, promoters claimed that returns were supported in part by large-scale cryptocurrency mining operations. The SEC complaint alleges that:

- HyperTech was promoted as a crypto-mining and blockchain-technology group.
- Sam Lee later admitted that HyperTech was not engaged in large-scale bitcoin mining.
- HyperFund had no legitimate revenue source sufficient to support the promised returns.
- Investor withdrawals were allegedly funded with deposits from newer investors. [SRC-004]

The DOJ likewise states that the alleged mining operations did not exist. [SRC-002]

**Assessment:** If the allegations are proven, the claimed mining-based revenue model would have functioned as a credibility narrative rather than the actual source of investor payments. The alleged use of new investor deposits to satisfy withdrawals is the central Ponzi-like mechanism described by the SEC.

---

## 3. Recruitment and multi-level marketing structure

The evidence describes two overlapping ways investors were allegedly encouraged to participate:

- Passive rewards for purchasing a membership.
- Accelerated or leveraged rewards for recruiting additional investors.

The SEC complaint alleges that investors purchased memberships using Tether, receiving internal “HyperUnits.” It describes community, VIP, and global reward programs tied to recruitment and organizational volume. One alleged community program paid rewards based on a downline extending up to 20 levels. [SRC-004]

The Guardian likewise reported that members received HyperUnits for recruiting new members, with referral commissions calculated according to the number of recruits and additional recruits made by those participants, extending down to 20 levels. [SRC-003]

The SEC complaint also alleges that promoters encouraged “rebuys,” in which members reinvested rewards instead of withdrawing them. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The alleged structure combined investment returns with recruitment-based compensation. That combination is consistent with the pyramid-scheme characterization made by the SEC and DOJ, although the legal determination depends on the relevant court proceedings.

---

## 4. Token and withdrawal mechanics

The SEC complaint alleges that:

1. Investors used Tether to purchase membership packages.
2. Their account balances were represented internally as HyperUnits.
3. To withdraw, HyperUnits had to be converted into MOF.
4. MOF had to be transferred through the HOO Exchange and converted into other crypto assets before being exchanged for fiat currency.
5. HyperUnits were initially represented as pegged to a dollar value, but the MOF conversion was not pegged at that value.
6. MOF was quoted at approximately **$0.00001949** on September 4, 2023, according to the complaint. [SRC-004]

The DOJ alleges that investor withdrawals began to be blocked by at least July 2021. [SRC-002] CNBC also reports that the scheme collapsed in 2022. [SRC-001]

**Assessment:** The described architecture could create a substantial gap between an investor’s nominal account balance and the realizable withdrawal value. It also introduced additional conversion steps and platform dependencies, potentially increasing friction and limiting liquidity. The evidence establishes these allegations and reported mechanics, but does not independently establish the full transaction history of each investor.

## 5. Public promoters and credibility-based recruitment

### Brenda Chunga / “Bitcoin Beautee”

The SEC identifies Brenda Chunga, also known as **“Bitcoin Beautee,”** as one of HyperFund’s top promoters and a prominent figure in its U.S. promotional activity. The complaint alleges that:

- She promoted daily passive rewards and accelerated rewards.
- She reached the highest promoter level within six months.
- That level allegedly required at least $5 million in new investments referred as “sales.”
- She received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors.
- She used apparent wealth and extravagant personal spending to help recruit others. [SRC-004]

CNBC reports that Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud and separately agreed to settle SEC civil charges. [SRC-001] The DOJ also states that she pleaded guilty. [SRC-002]

The SEC complaint further alleges that Chunga’s presentations used founders’ public profiles and media appearances as credibility signals. The presentations reportedly emphasized CNN appearances, publicly traded companies, Amazon Prime exposure, and the argument that the founders had “more to lose than to gain.” [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** Chunga appears in the evidence as both a high-volume recruiter and a credibility amplifier. Her alleged use of visible wealth and founder publicity illustrates how the scheme could convert social proof into investment confidence.

### Rodney Burton / “Bitcoin Rodney”

The DOJ identifies Rodney Burton, also known as **“Bitcoin Rodney,”** as a promoter of HyperFund. He was charged with conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money-transmitting business and operating an unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

The available benchmark material provides less detail about Burton’s specific recruitment messaging than it does about Chunga. His alleged role should therefore be described as a promoter and charged participant, without attributing additional tactics not documented in the sources.

## 6. The questionable CEO persona

### Steven Reece Lewis

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis was introduced as HyperVerse’s CEO at a December 2021 online launch event. Promotional material attributed to him claimed:

- A University of Leeds degree.
- A master’s degree from the University of Cambridge.
- Employment at Goldman Sachs.
- The sale of a web-development company to Adobe.
- The creation of an IT start-up. [SRC-003]

The Guardian states that it found:

- No record of Steven Reece Lewis at the University of Leeds or University of Cambridge.
- No record under that name in UK Companies House or SEC records.
- No Adobe filing showing acquisition of a company owned by him.
- No Goldman Sachs employment record.
- No LinkedIn profile or meaningful internet presence outside HyperVerse promotional material. [SRC-003]

The Guardian also reported that the account in his name appeared shortly before the launch, promoted HyperVerse for approximately six months, and then became inactive. [SRC-003]

Separately, the SEC complaint alleges that HyperTech hired an actor to pretend to be the new HyperVerse CEO. The complaint does not, in the supplied text, independently prove that Steven Reece Lewis was the actor; that connection should therefore remain an allegation or unresolved inference. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The evidence supports describing the CEO identity and credentials as **questionable and unverified**, not as conclusively fabricated. The strongest formulation is that the Guardian could not verify the claimed background and the SEC separately alleged the use of an actor as a supposed CEO.

---

## 7. Celebrity and public-image promotion

The Guardian reported that HyperVerse released support videos featuring:

- Steve Wozniak
- Chuck Norris
- Jim Norton
- Lance Bass [SRC-003]

The reported messages encouraged support for HyperVerse and praised or endorsed Steven Reece Lewis’s leadership. The Guardian noted that all four individuals were available through Cameo, a service allowing users to commission personalized videos, and that the messages appeared during a broader recruitment push. [SRC-003]

The Guardian explicitly stated that there was **no suggestion these celebrities knew the underlying business model**. The videos did not refer to investments or money, according to the report. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The videos could function as social-proof and legitimacy signals even if the participants did not understand or endorse the alleged investment mechanics. The evidence supports the existence of the promotional videos, but not intentional participation in fraud by the celebrities.

## 8. Collapse and investor harm

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund collapsed in 2022 when investors could no longer make withdrawals. [SRC-004]

The DOJ alleges that withdrawal blocking began by at least July 2021. [SRC-002]

The Guardian reported that thousands of people lost millions of dollars and cited a Chainalysis estimate of approximately **$1.3 billion in consumer losses during 2022**, although that estimate is presented by the Guardian and is distinct from the SEC’s alleged amount raised. [SRC-003]

The SEC alleges that the operation raised more than $1.7 billion, while DOJ and CNBC describe the criminal case as involving approximately $1.89 billion. These figures may reflect different methodologies, periods, or legal allegations. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

## 9. Integrated assessment: how the alleged system worked

The benchmark evidence supports the following investigative model:

1. **Credibility construction:** HyperTech, its founders, claimed mining operations, media appearances, celebrity videos, and a purported CEO were used to present the project as technologically sophisticated and socially validated. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

2. **High-return proposition:** Investors were offered unusually high, largely passive daily returns and the prospect of doubling or tripling principal. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

3. **Recruitment expansion:** Investors were encouraged to bring in friends, family, and downline participants, with multi-level commissions and additional rewards. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

4. **Retention and reinvestment:** “Rebuys” and internal account balances encouraged investors to leave funds within the system rather than withdraw. [SRC-004]

5. **Liquidity restriction:** Withdrawal required conversion through internal units, MOF, and an associated exchange, while the alleged value of the internal units was not maintained during conversion. [SRC-004]

6. **Rebranding during distress:** As withdrawal problems emerged, the operation shifted from HyperFund to HyperVerse and then HyperNation, preserving an apparent sense of continuity or renewal. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

7. **Narrative replacement:** The project’s stated themes shifted from DeFi and mining to the metaverse and a masked, quasi-political “new world order” presentation. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Overall assessment:** The evidence depicts an alleged recruitment-driven financial system in which high promised returns, referral incentives, public-facing personalities, celebrity association, changing brand identities, and an apparently unverifiable executive persona collectively reduced investor skepticism and supported continued inflows. The SEC and DOJ allegations describe the economic core as dependent on investor deposits rather than legitimate mining revenue. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

---

## 10. Key uncertainties and limitations

- The SEC complaint contains allegations, not final findings on every factual issue. [SRC-004]
- The DOJ states that criminal defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. [SRC-002]
- The SEC’s alleged total of over $1.7 billion and the DOJ/CNBC figure of approximately $1.89 billion are not identical and should not be merged without qualification. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]
- The Guardian’s inability to verify Steven Reece Lewis’s credentials does not alone prove that the identity was fictitious.
- The SEC allegation that an actor was hired to pose as CEO does not, in the supplied evidence, conclusively identify Lewis as that actor. [SRC-004]
- The celebrity videos establish promotional association, not knowledge of or intent to support the alleged fraud. [SRC-003]
- The available evidence gives substantially more detail about Brenda Chunga’s promotional activity than Rodney Burton’s specific messaging.

# Final OSINT Report: HyperFund / HyperVerse Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence describes HyperFund—later associated with the names HyperVerse and HyperNation—as an alleged global crypto-asset pyramid and Ponzi scheme. According to the SEC complaint, the operation raised more than **$1.7 billion** through membership packages that promised unusually high daily returns and rewarded investors for recruiting additional participants. The DOJ characterized the criminal case as involving an alleged **$1.89 billion** cryptocurrency fraud scheme. These figures differ slightly by source and should not be treated as a single independently verified total. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

The alleged recruitment model combined:

1. **High-return investment promises**—including advertised daily returns of 0.5% to 1% and potential doubling or tripling of principal.
2. **Multi-level referral incentives**—including commissions linked to direct and multi-level recruitment.
3. **Credibility marketing**—emphasizing founders’ media appearances, public profiles, and purported business affiliations.
4. **Public promoters**—particularly Brenda Chunga (“Bitcoin Beautee”) and Rodney Burton (“Bitcoin Rodney”).
5. **Rebranding and migration**—from HyperFund to HyperVerse and later HyperNation.
6. **A questionable CEO persona**—Steven Reece Lewis, whose qualifications and employment history could not be verified by the Guardian, while the SEC complaint alleges an actor was hired to pose as HyperVerse’s CEO.
7. **Withdrawal restrictions and token conversion mechanisms**—which allegedly made it difficult for investors to recover the nominal value of their holdings.

The criminal charges and SEC allegations are not equivalent to final judicial findings against every defendant. The DOJ expressly notes the presumption of innocence. Brenda Chunga, however, pleaded guilty according to the DOJ and CNBC reports. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 1. Identity and organizational continuity

### HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation

The SEC complaint states that HyperFund was launched by the HyperTech Group in June 2020, rebranded as **HyperVerse** around December 2021, and later as **HyperNation** around May 2022. The DOJ describes the alleged network as also known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

This supports treating the names as successive or associated iterations of one alleged operation, rather than clearly separate enterprises. The SEC described the projects collectively as “HyperFund,” while the DOJ used a set of associated names. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

### Rebranding pattern

The SEC alleges that the project’s stated goals changed over time and used different contemporary themes, including decentralized finance, the metaverse, and a decentralized government concept associated with HyperNation. [SRC-004]

The Guardian reported that members experiencing withdrawal problems were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. A senior promoter reportedly described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” although that characterization came from the promoter and is not independently established by the source. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The available evidence supports a pattern of continuity through renaming and migration. It does not, by itself, establish the precise legal or corporate structure connecting each iteration.

---

## 2. Alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Promised returns

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund membership packages promised returns of **0.5% to 1% per day**, with the possibility of tripling the initial investment in 600 days. [SRC-004]

The Guardian similarly reported a minimum membership of **$300**, a minimum return of 0.5% per day, and a purported 300% return over 600 days. [SRC-003]

The DOJ states that promotional materials allegedly promised daily passive rewards of 0.5% to 1% until the investor’s initial investment was doubled or tripled. [SRC-002]

### Claimed source of returns

According to the SEC and DOJ allegations, promoters claimed that returns were supported in part by large-scale cryptocurrency mining operations. The SEC complaint alleges that:

- HyperTech was promoted as a crypto-mining and blockchain-technology group.
- Sam Lee later admitted that HyperTech was not engaged in large-scale bitcoin mining.
- HyperFund had no legitimate revenue source sufficient to support the promised returns.
- Investor withdrawals were allegedly funded with deposits from newer investors. [SRC-004]

The DOJ likewise states that the alleged mining operations did not exist. [SRC-002]

**Assessment:** If the allegations are proven, the claimed mining-based revenue model would have functioned as a credibility narrative rather than the actual source of investor payments. The alleged use of new investor deposits to satisfy withdrawals is the central Ponzi-like mechanism described by the SEC.

---

## 3. Recruitment and multi-level marketing structure

The evidence describes two overlapping ways investors were allegedly encouraged to participate:

- Passive rewards for purchasing a membership.
- Accelerated or leveraged rewards for recruiting additional investors.

The SEC complaint alleges that investors purchased memberships using Tether, receiving internal “HyperUnits.” It describes community, VIP, and global reward programs tied to recruitment and organizational volume. One alleged community program paid rewards based on a downline extending up to 20 levels. [SRC-004]

The Guardian likewise reported that members received HyperUnits for recruiting new members, with referral commissions calculated according to the number of recruits and additional recruits made by those participants, extending down to 20 levels. [SRC-003]

The SEC complaint also alleges that promoters encouraged “rebuys,” in which members reinvested rewards instead of withdrawing them. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The alleged structure combined investment returns with recruitment-based compensation. That combination is consistent with the pyramid-scheme characterization made by the SEC and DOJ, although the legal determination depends on the relevant court proceedings.

---

## 4. Token and withdrawal mechanics

The SEC complaint alleges that:

1. Investors used Tether to purchase membership packages.
2. Their account balances were represented internally as HyperUnits.
3. To withdraw, HyperUnits had to be converted into MOF.
4. MOF had to be transferred through the HOO Exchange and converted into other crypto assets before being exchanged for fiat currency.
5. HyperUnits were initially represented as pegged to a dollar value, but the MOF conversion was not pegged at that value.
6. MOF was quoted at approximately **$0.00001949** on September 4, 2023, according to the complaint. [SRC-004]

The DOJ alleges that investor withdrawals began to be blocked by at least July 2021. [SRC-002] CNBC also reports that the scheme collapsed in 2022. [SRC-001]

**Assessment:** The described architecture could create a substantial gap between an investor’s nominal account balance and the realizable withdrawal value. It also introduced additional conversion steps and platform dependencies, potentially increasing friction and limiting liquidity. The evidence establishes these allegations and reported mechanics, but does not independently establish the full transaction history of each investor.

---

## 5. Public promoters and credibility-based recruitment

### Brenda Chunga / “Bitcoin Beautee”

The SEC identifies Brenda Chunga, also known as **“Bitcoin Beautee,”** as one of HyperFund’s top promoters and a prominent figure in its U.S. promotional activity. The complaint alleges that:

- She promoted daily passive rewards and accelerated rewards.
- She reached the highest promoter level within six months.
- That level allegedly required at least $5 million in new investments referred as “sales.”
- She received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors.
- She used apparent wealth and extravagant personal spending to help recruit others. [SRC-004]

CNBC reports that Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud and separately agreed to settle SEC civil charges. [SRC-001] The DOJ also states that she pleaded guilty. [SRC-002]

The SEC complaint further alleges that Chunga’s presentations used founders’ public profiles and media appearances as credibility signals. The presentations reportedly emphasized CNN appearances, publicly traded companies, Amazon Prime exposure, and the argument that the founders had “more to lose than to gain.” [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** Chunga appears in the evidence as both a high-volume recruiter and a credibility amplifier. Her alleged use of visible wealth and founder publicity illustrates how the scheme could convert social proof into investment confidence.

### Rodney Burton / “Bitcoin Rodney”

The DOJ identifies Rodney Burton, also known as **“Bitcoin Rodney,”** as a promoter of HyperFund. He was charged with conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money-transmitting business and operating an unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

The available benchmark material provides less detail about Burton’s specific recruitment messaging than it does about Chunga. His alleged role should therefore be described as a promoter and charged participant, without attributing additional tactics not documented in the sources.

---

## 6. The questionable CEO persona

### Steven Reece Lewis

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis was introduced as HyperVerse’s CEO at a December 2021 online launch event. Promotional material attributed to him claimed:

- A University of Leeds degree.
- A master’s degree from the University of Cambridge.
- Employment at Goldman Sachs.
- The sale of a web-development company to Adobe.
- The creation of an IT start-up. [SRC-003]

The Guardian states that it found:

- No record of Steven Reece Lewis at the University of Leeds or University of Cambridge.
- No record under that name in UK Companies House or SEC records.
- No Adobe filing showing acquisition of a company owned by him.
- No Goldman Sachs employment record.
- No LinkedIn profile or meaningful internet presence outside HyperVerse promotional material. [SRC-003]

The Guardian also reported that the account in his name appeared shortly before the launch, promoted HyperVerse for approximately six months, and then became inactive. [SRC-003]

Separately, the SEC complaint alleges that HyperTech hired an actor to pretend to be the new HyperVerse CEO. The complaint does not, in the supplied text, independently prove that Steven Reece Lewis was the actor; that connection should therefore remain an allegation or unresolved inference. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The evidence supports describing the CEO identity and credentials as **questionable and unverified**, not as conclusively fabricated. The strongest formulation is that the Guardian could not verify the claimed background and the SEC separately alleged the use of an actor as a supposed CEO.

---

## 7. Celebrity and public-image promotion

The Guardian reported that HyperVerse released support videos featuring:

- Steve Wozniak
- Chuck Norris
- Jim Norton
- Lance Bass [SRC-003]

The reported messages encouraged support for HyperVerse and praised or endorsed Steven Reece Lewis’s leadership. The Guardian noted that all four individuals were available through Cameo, a service allowing users to commission personalized videos, and that the messages appeared during a broader recruitment push. [SRC-003]

The Guardian explicitly stated that there was **no suggestion these celebrities knew the underlying business model**. The videos did not refer to investments or money, according to the report. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The videos could function as social-proof and legitimacy signals even if the participants did not understand or endorse the alleged investment mechanics. The evidence supports the existence of the promotional videos, but not intentional participation in fraud by the celebrities.

---

## 8. Collapse and investor harm

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund collapsed in 2022 when investors could no longer make withdrawals. [SRC-004]

The DOJ alleges that withdrawal blocking began by at least July 2021. [SRC-002]

The Guardian reported that thousands of people lost millions of dollars and cited a Chainalysis estimate of approximately **$1.3 billion in consumer losses during 2022**, although that estimate is presented by the Guardian and is distinct from the SEC’s alleged amount raised. [SRC-003]

The SEC alleges that the operation raised more than $1.7 billion, while DOJ and CNBC describe the criminal case as involving approximately $1.89 billion. These figures may reflect different methodologies, periods, or legal allegations. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 9. Integrated assessment: how the alleged system worked

The benchmark evidence supports the following investigative model:

1. **Credibility construction:** HyperTech, its founders, claimed mining operations, media appearances, celebrity videos, and a purported CEO were used to present the project as technologically sophisticated and socially validated. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

2. **High-return proposition:** Investors were offered unusually high, largely passive daily returns and the prospect of doubling or tripling principal. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

3. **Recruitment expansion:** Investors were encouraged to bring in friends, family, and downline participants, with multi-level commissions and additional rewards. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

4. **Retention and reinvestment:** “Rebuys” and internal account balances encouraged investors to leave funds within the system rather than withdraw. [SRC-004]

5. **Liquidity restriction:** Withdrawal required conversion through internal units, MOF, and an associated exchange, while the alleged value of the internal units was not maintained during conversion. [SRC-004]

6. **Rebranding during distress:** As withdrawal problems emerged, the operation shifted from HyperFund to HyperVerse and then HyperNation, preserving an apparent sense of continuity or renewal. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

7. **Narrative replacement:** The project’s stated themes shifted from DeFi and mining to the metaverse and a masked, quasi-political “new world order” presentation. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Overall assessment:** The evidence depicts an alleged recruitment-driven financial system in which high promised returns, referral incentives, public-facing personalities, celebrity association, changing brand identities, and an apparently unverifiable executive persona collectively reduced investor skepticism and supported continued inflows. The SEC and DOJ allegations describe the economic core as dependent on investor deposits rather than legitimate mining revenue. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

---

## 10. Key uncertainties and limitations

- The SEC complaint contains allegations, not final findings on every factual issue. [SRC-004]
- The DOJ states that criminal defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. [SRC-002]
- The SEC’s alleged total of over $1.7 billion and the DOJ/CNBC figure of approximately $1.89 billion are not identical and should not be merged without qualification. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]
- The Guardian’s inability to verify Steven Reece Lewis’s credentials does not alone prove that the identity was fictitious.
- The SEC allegation that an actor was hired to pose as CEO does not, in the supplied evidence, conclusively identify Lewis as that actor. [SRC-004]
- The celebrity videos establish promotional association, not knowledge of or intent to support the alleged fraud. [SRC-003]
- The available evidence gives substantially more detail about Brenda Chunga’s promotional activity than Rodney Burton’s specific messaging.

The Guardian reported that it could not verify those claims in university, corporate, SEC, employment, or internet records. The SEC separately alleges that HyperTech hired an actor to pretend to be the HyperVerse CEO, but the supplied evidence does not conclusively establish that Lewis was that actor.

key_findings.question: How were celebrities used?
key_findings.answer: The Guardian reports that Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass appeared in support videos promoting HyperVerse. The report also states there was no suggestion that they knew the alleged business model or that the videos concerned investments.

key_findings.question: What withdrawal and token mechanisms are alleged?
key_findings.answer: The SEC alleges that investors purchased memberships with Tether, received internal HyperUnits, and had to convert them to MOF and use the HOO Exchange before converting to other crypto assets or fiat. The complaint alleges that the conversion was not pegged to the nominal HyperUnit value and that MOF had fallen to approximately $0.00001949 by September 4, 2023.

key_findings.question: What happened during the collapse?
key_findings.answer: The DOJ alleges that withdrawals began to be blocked by at least July 2021. The SEC says the scheme collapsed in 2022 when investors could no longer withdraw funds. The Guardian reports that many investors were unable to access their funds and that some were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation.

contradictions.description: The SEC alleges that HyperFund raised over $1.7 billion, while the DOJ and CNBC describe an alleged $1.89 billion scheme. The sources do not explain whether the difference reflects different time periods, entities, methodologies, or charge calculations.

The SEC complaint alleges that an actor was hired to pretend to be the HyperVerse CEO, while the Guardian identifies Steven Reece Lewis as the person presented as CEO but reports only that his identity and credentials could not be verified. The supplied evidence does not conclusively establish that Lewis was the alleged actor.

HyperFund's presentation materials allegedly emphasized crypto mining as a revenue source, while the SEC and DOJ allege that no large-scale mining operation existed. This is an allegation about the business model, not a final adjudicated finding in the supplied materials.

Sam Lee was described in promotional and investigative material as centrally involved or a co-founder, while Lee denied being the founder or being involved in HyperNation. The supplied evidence does not resolve the full extent of his role in every rebranded iteration.

reasoning_step_details.conclusion: The alleged operation used a recruitment-dependent economic model rather than relying solely on passive investment returns.
The alleged mining narrative appears central to the claimed justification for returns, while the SEC and DOJ allege that the mining operations did not exist.
Public visibility was allegedly used as a substitute for transparent financial verification: founder media exposure, celebrity videos, and the purported CEO were presented as credibility signals.
Rebranding and migration may have helped preserve recruitment momentum after withdrawal problems, although the exact legal continuity among the entities remains uncertain.
The alleged internal-unit and token-conversion process could have obscured the difference between nominal account balances and realizable withdrawal value.

Rodney Burton, also known as Bitcoin Rodney, was identified by DOJ as a promoter and charged with unlicensed money-transmitting offenses.
